question.problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x={t}^{2},\,y=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}{t}^{4},\,t\in [0,\sqrt[4]{6}].
$$

Determine the surface area $S$ generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis. Do not round the answer.

$S=$
{{field-1}}
question.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=\sqrt[4]{6}.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})=2t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}{t}^{4})=\frac{4}{\sqrt{3}}{t}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[4]{6}}{t}^{2}\sqrt{(2t)^{2}+{(\frac{4}{\sqrt{3}}{t}^{3})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[4]{6}}{t}^{2}\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+\frac{16}{3}{t}^{6}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[4]{6}}{t}^{2}\sqrt{4{t}^{2}(1+\frac{4}{3}{t}^{4})}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[4]{6}}{t}^{2}\cdot 2|t|\sqrt{1+\frac{4}{3}{t}^{4}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =4\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[4]{6}}\sqrt{1+\frac{4}{3}{t}^{4}}\cdot {t}^{3}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the last integral using the substitution $u=1+\frac{4}{3}{t}^{4}.$ Then, $\text{d}u=\frac{16}{3}{t}^{3}\,\text{d}t⟹{t}^{3}\,\text{d}t=\frac{3}{16}\text{d}u.$ We also update the limits of integration for $u:$

| **$t$** | $0$ | $\sqrt[4]{6}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $9$ |

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =4\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[4]{6}}\sqrt{1+\frac{4}{3}{t}^{4}}\cdot {t}^{3}\,\text{d}t \\  & =4\pi {\int }_{1}^{9}\sqrt{u}\cdot \frac{3}{16}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3\pi }{4}{\int }_{1}^{9}{u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3\pi }{4}\cdot {[\frac{2}{3}{u}^{3/2}]}_{1}^{9} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}[(9)^{3/2}-(1)^{3/2}] \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}(27-1) \\  & =13\pi .\end{aligned}
$$
